rationale: B wins because it treats the weak spot as the story, not a footnote. Its headline, "Khan Academy's AI tutor reaches 1 million more students before the research is in," gives a reporter tension, timing, and a clean evidence question; A's "Free AI lesson-planning help arrives for teachers already stretched thin" wanders into generic teacher-burnout furniture the update did not supply. A has good bones, but B is sharper about what must be proved before anyone opens their mouth.
gaps_in_A: "while rivals still charge for it" asserts a competitor-pricing contrast the update does not give. Asking for proof later does not fully clean up the headline.
"Free AI lesson-planning help arrives for teachers already stretched thin" adds a workload/burnout premise not in the update, then admits there is no time-saved or workload data.
"which tends to center on students" invents prior-coverage context. If you have not checked coverage, do not pretend you know the pattern.
The refused local-news angle is too quick to kill: "which 30 districts are getting Khanmigo" could become real if Khan provides named districts. The right label is under-sourced, not duplicate.
gaps_in_B: "competitors sell" is still an asserted market contrast not present in the update, even though the proof section later warns not to assert unverified competitor pricing.
"a nonprofit with unusual credibility" imports reputation context outside the supplied facts. It is probably true in the real world; that is exactly why it needed sourcing.
"hand a chatbot to a classroom" is punchy, but the update calls Khanmigo an AI tutor. Do not casually swap in "chatbot" unless the product interaction supports it.

The next step says "journalist-fit-check," then immediately says to get the methodology first. The real next step is proof acquisition/fact-check; reporter targeting comes after the evidence spine is solid.
